Two rays meet the same glass–air boundary: the shallow one gets out, the steep one is turned back inside.

About: Total Internal Reflection

Source

Topic
Geometric optics — refraction at a flat interface
Simulation
Single ray crossing dense→rare boundary
Concept
Above the critical angle, no refracted ray exists — all light reflects.
Serves
Snell's law, critical angle, TIR condition (n₁ > n₂), applications (fibre optics, prisms)
Misconception target
Students expect a "grazing" refracted ray to persist at exactly θ_c and just past — in fact the refracted ray vanishes.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The setup

A light ray sits in the DENSER medium (say, glass, n₁=1.50) below a horizontal interface with air (n₂=1.00) above. Angles are measured from the dashed NORMAL, not from the surface.

Drag θ₁ in the sidebar. Watch what happens at the interface for a small angle (e.g. 20°).

2 · Predict — increase θ₁

You slowly increase θ₁ from 20° toward 90°. What happens to the REFRACTED ray in the air above?

3 · Observe — at θ_c

θ₁ is now at the critical angle: 41.81° for n₁=1.50, n₂=1.00, the value in the θ_c readout. The refracted ray lies flat ALONG the interface — θ₂ = 90.00°.

It has also gone almost dark. Each ray is drawn with the share of the light it carries, and at θ_c the transmitted share has fallen to zero while the reflected ray has taken all of it.

4 · Predict — go past θ_c

Now push θ₁ just past θ_c. What does the refracted ray do?

5 · The condition

Two things are required for TIR:

① Light must be going from a denser to a rarer medium (n₁ > n₂). Try flipping to n₁=1.00, n₂=1.50 — the θ_c readout shows "— (none)" and the Regime reads "rare→dense (no TIR)". Sweep θ₁ all the way to 89°: the refracted ray never leaves.

② The angle of incidence must exceed θ_c = arcsin(n₂/n₁).

6 · Free exploration

Vary n₁, n₂, and θ₁ freely. Watch the θ_c readout track the ratio n₂/n₁. Try:

• Water (n₁=1.33) → air: θ_c ≈ 48.8° — this is why a fish looks up through a circular "window".

• Diamond (n₁=2.42) → air: θ_c ≈ 24.4° — small critical angle means diamond traps light easily, hence its sparkle.

01

At a glance

A ray of light travels in a lower medium of refractive index n₁ and meets a flat boundary with an upper medium of index n₂. You choose the angle of incidence θ₁, n₁ and n₂, and the sim draws what the boundary does to the ray.

What you'll learn

  • How Snell's law links the angles on the two sides of a boundary.
  • How the light is divided between the refracted ray and the reflected ray.
  • How that division depends on θ₁ and on the two refractive indices.
  • Where the idea is used, from binoculars to optical fibres.
The set-up as drawn, with the incident ray only. Angles are measured from the normal.

What's on screen

  • Pink ray: the incident ray, coming up from below.
  • Blue ray: the refracted ray, the part of the light that crosses the boundary.
  • Amber ray: the reflected ray, which goes back down. Each ray is labelled with its share of the light.
  • Readouts panel: four live values for the ray at the boundary.
See itLook at the boundary with the opening values. Watch for: the pink incident ray, the dashed normal, and the blue and amber rays leaving the strike point.

03

Snell's law gives the refracted angle

At the boundary the angle of the refracted ray, θ₂, follows from the angle of incidence and the two indices:

n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
Both angles are measured from the normal.
  • The reflected ray leaves at the same angle as the incident one: θ_r = θ₁.
  • When n₁ is greater than n₂, sin θ₂ is larger than sin θ₁. The refracted ray then leans away from the normal.
  • Going into a denser medium, with n₁ less than n₂, it leans toward the normal instead.
θ₁10°20°30°40°
θ₂15.10°30.87°48.59°74.62°
sin θ₂ / sin θ₁1.501.501.501.50

For n₁ = 1.50 and n₂ = 1.00. The ratio is n₁/n₂ every time.

See itWalk θ₁ from 10° up to 40°, with glass below and air above. Watch for: θ₂ climbing from 15.10° to 74.62°, always larger than θ₁.
04

At the critical angle the refracted ray skims the surface

As θ₁ grows, θ₂ grows faster, so some θ₁ makes θ₂ equal to 90°. That θ₁ is the critical angle θ_c. Putting θ₂ = 90° into Snell's law gives

sin θ_c = n₂ / n₁
This holds only when n₁ is greater than n₂.
  • For glass into air, sin θ_c = 1/1.50, so θ_c = 41.81°.
  • The sim draws each ray with a thickness that shows its share of the light. For glass into air the reflected share is 4% at small angles, 25% at 40° and 89% at 41.8°.
  • So the refracted ray fades as it swings flat, instead of switching off.
  • The slider moves in steps of 0.1°, so the nearest setting is 41.8°. There θ₂ = 88.85° and the regime reads "at θ_c".
See itWalk θ₁ from 30° up to 41.8°, with glass below and air above. Watch for: the blue ray swinging nearly flat and faint, with θ₂ = 88.85°.
05

Past the critical angle all the light is reflected

For θ₁ above θ_c, Snell's law would need sin θ₂ = (n₁/n₂) sin θ₁, which is larger than 1. No angle has a sine above 1, so no refracted ray exists.

  • All the light stays in the first medium. This is total internal reflection, or TIR.
  • The reflected ray leaves at θ_r = θ₁ and carries 100% of the light.
  • The sim then shows a TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION banner, lists θ₂ as "— (TIR)" and names the regime "TIR (θ₁ > θ_c)".
  • Even 0.1° past θ_c, at θ₁ = 41.9°, the blue ray is already gone.
θ₁40°41.8°41.9°60°
θ₂74.62°88.85°nonenone
reflected25%89%100%100%

For n₁ = 1.50 and n₂ = 1.00.

See itWalk θ₁ from 40° to 50°, with glass below and air above. Watch for: the blue ray vanishing as θ₁ passes 41.81°, then the banner and "Reflected 100%".
06

TIR needs a path from a denser to a rarer medium

Two conditions must hold together. The light must go from the higher index to the lower one, n₁ greater than n₂. And θ₁ must exceed θ_c = arcsin(n₂/n₁).

  • If n₁ is less than n₂, then (n₁/n₂) sin θ₁ is below 1 for every θ₁, so a refracted ray always exists.
  • For air into glass, n₁ = 1.00 and n₂ = 1.50, θ₂ never passes 41.80°, even at θ₁ = 89°. That is the glass-to-air θ_c, because the two paths are the same ray run backwards.
  • The sim then reads "— (none)" for θ_c and "rare→dense (no TIR)" for the regime.
  • If n₁ = n₂, the ray does not bend at all.
See itSet n₁ = 1.00 and n₂ = 1.50, then walk θ₁ from 0° to 89°. Watch for: θ₂ stopping at 41.80°, with θ_c reading "— (none)".
07

The critical angle falls as n₁ rises

Since sin θ_c = n₂/n₁, a larger n₁ gives a smaller θ_c, and a larger n₂ gives a larger one. Light is trapped more easily in a high-index material.

Pathn₁, n₂θ_c
water to air1.33, 1.0048.75°
glass to air1.50, 1.0041.81°
diamond to air2.42, 1.0024.41°
glass to water1.50, 1.3362.46°
  • Diamond's small θ_c means much of the light inside meets a face beyond θ_c and is reflected again, which adds to its sparkle.
  • At θ₁ = 30° with air above, TIR starts once n₁ passes 2.00, because sin θ_c = 1/n₁ then equals sin 30°.
See itHold θ₁ at 30° with n₂ = 1.00, and raise n₁ from 1.33 to 2.42. Watch for: θ_c falling from 48.75° to 24.41°, and TIR switching on once n₁ passes 2.00.
08

Where it matters

  • Optical fibres. Light stays inside a glass core because it meets the boundary with the cladding beyond θ_c. For a core of index 1.48 and a cladding of 1.46, θ_c = 80.57°, so guided rays run within about 9.4° of the fibre's axis.
  • Prisms in binoculars and periscopes. A ray meets the inside of a 45° glass face at 45°, which is above 41.81°. It reflects with no silvering.
  • Diamonds and cut glass. The small θ_c of diamond keeps light inside until it leaves through the top.
  • A fish's view. From under water the whole sky is squeezed into a cone of full angle 2 × 48.75° = 97.5°. Outside it the surface acts as a mirror.
Go deeper: the light does not stop dead at the boundary

Even in total reflection, an evanescent wave reaches about one wavelength into the upper medium. It carries no energy away. If a second surface comes that close, some light crosses the gap, which is called frustrated total internal reflection. Optical fingerprint readers use this.

09

Summary

In one line. A ray that meets the boundary between two media is divided between a refracted ray and a reflected ray, in a way set by the angle of incidence and the two refractive indices.

Key points

  • n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, with both angles measured from the normal, and θ_r = θ₁.
  • sin θ_c = n₂/n₁, and it exists only when n₁ is greater than n₂.
  • For θ₁ above θ_c there is no refracted ray, and all the light is reflected.
  • Total internal reflection needs both a denser-to-rarer path and θ₁ above θ_c.

Common mix-ups

  • "Just past θ_c the refracted ray grazes the surface." It disappears completely.
  • "Light going from air into glass can be totally reflected at a steep angle." It cannot, because there is no critical angle in that direction.
  • "The angles are measured from the surface." They are measured from the normal.

Things to try on your own

  • With n₂ = 1.00, find the n₁ that gives θ_c = 30°.
  • With n₁ = 1.50, find the n₂ that gives θ_c = 60°.
  • With n₁ = 1.00 and n₂ = 2.50, find the largest θ₂ you can reach.
